Thank you dear subscribers, we are overwhelmed with your response. Your Turn is a unique section from ThePrint featuring points of view from its subscribers. If you are a subscriber, have a point of view, please send it to us. If not, do subscribe here: https://theprint.in/subscribe/
India’s cities rarely stop working. Construction continues, food is delivered, streets are cleaned and markets remain open even when temperatures become dangerous. But behind this image of urban resilience lies a question that receives insufficient attention: who pays the price of keeping the economy running during extreme heat? For millions of Indians who depend on outdoor and informal employment, extreme heat is no longer merely a seasonal inconvenience. It is a question of livelihood, occupational safety and economic justice. A salaried employee working in an air-conditioned office may have the option of working remotely or taking leave. A construction worker, street vendor, sanitation worker or delivery rider often has no such choice. For these workers, stopping work can mean losing the income needed to feed a family.
India’s heatwave crisis is therefore not simply an environmental problem. It is a labour crisis shaped by economic inequality.
The price of working in the heat
The economic consequences are substantial. A 2026 report by the International Institute for Environment and Development, titled Too Hot to Work, Too Poor to Rest, examined 538 informal-worker households in Delhi, Agra and Ajmer. It estimated that outdoor workers lose approximately 24 working days annually because of heat, equivalent to nearly one-tenth of their annual earnings. Its national modelling estimated heat-related productivity losses at around 1.41 per cent of India’s GDP. These figures reveal a dimension of climate vulnerability that conventional discussions of temperature records and disaster preparedness often overlook. Heat affects not only the body but also the ability to earn. When workers reduce their hours to avoid dangerous conditions, their incomes may decline. When they continue working, they risk dehydration, heat exhaustion and potentially life-threatening heatstroke. Neither option is economically secure.
The problem extends beyond immediate physical discomfort. Lost earnings can force households to reduce spending on food, education and healthcare. Workers living in poorly ventilated housing may have little opportunity to recover after a day in the heat. Migrant workers and those without adequate social protection face additional difficulties accessing healthcare and public services. Heat-related vulnerability is thus cumulative. The worker who cannot afford to stop working may also lack access to effective cooling at home, reliable healthcare and sufficient savings to absorb a temporary loss of income.
Government advisories are not enough
The government has recognised the need for intervention. In April 2026, the Union Ministry of Labour and Employment issued a nationwide advisory urging states and union territories to introduce preventive measures for workers exposed to rising temperatures. Its recommendations included adjusting working hours, ensuring access to drinking water and shaded rest areas, and implementing other occupational safety measures. These interventions are necessary, but the central question is whether protection reaches workers consistently and can be enforced.
An advisory asking employers to provide rest breaks does not automatically guarantee that a daily-wage worker can take one without losing earnings. A recommendation to adjust working hours offers limited protection if contractors continue to demand the same output within shorter periods. Similarly, safety provisions designed around formal workplaces may fail to reach street vendors, delivery workers and other people whose working environments are dispersed across cities.
India needs a more comprehensive approach to occupational heat protection. States should establish clear, risk-based workplace heat standards, with requirements for drinking water, shaded or cooled rest areas, appropriate work-rest schedules and emergency medical assistance. Employers and contractors should be held accountable for implementing these safeguards, while labour departments should monitor compliance. Most importantly, protection must include income security. Workers should not have to choose between obeying safety instructions and earning enough to survive. Paid rest periods, appropriate wage protection during heat-related work suspensions and accessible compensation for occupational heat illness deserve serious consideration.
Digital platforms, municipal authorities and contractors must also share responsibility for workers whose employment arrangements fall outside conventional workplaces. Heat Action Plans should identify vulnerable occupational groups, specify who is responsible for their protection and establish mechanisms to assess whether interventions are working.
Climate adaptation must include economic justice
There is also a compelling economic case for these reforms. Protecting workers from extreme heat is not an obstacle to productivity. It helps sustain the workforce on which urban economies depend. When heat reduces working capacity, interrupts employment and increases healthcare costs, the consequences extend to households, businesses and public services. Preventive measures can reduce these losses while protecting human life. Governments should therefore treat occupational heat safety as an investment in economic resilience rather than an additional administrative burden.
The response must also be attentive to gender. Women working in agriculture, street vending, construction and other exposed occupations may face additional pressures from unpaid domestic work and caregiving. Their ability to recover from heat exposure can be constrained by responsibilities that continue long after paid employment ends. Heat policies must recognise these unequal burdens instead of treating workers as a homogeneous category. A meaningful adaptation strategy should connect workplace safeguards with public health, urban planning and social protection. It should ensure that workers can access drinking water, healthcare and cooling facilities, while strengthening the social security mechanisms that help households withstand income shocks.
India’s climate preparedness cannot be measured solely by the number of heat alerts issued, emergency meetings held or advisories circulated. It must also be measured by whether workers are protected when temperatures become dangerous, whether their wages are safeguarded when work becomes unsafe and whether employers are held accountable for preventable harm. The deeper issue is one of power. People with secure employment and adequate resources can often avoid the worst consequences of extreme heat. Those who depend on daily physical labour have fewer choices. Climate change intensifies this inequality, but insecure employment and inadequate protection determine how severely it is experienced.
India cannot build resilient cities by treating the suffering of outdoor workers as an unavoidable cost of economic growth. The people who construct its buildings, deliver its meals, clean its streets and sustain its markets should not have to risk their health to keep cities functioning.
The real test of India’s heat preparedness is not whether the government can warn citizens that temperatures are rising. It is whether a worker can stop working when the heat becomes dangerous without sacrificing the income needed to survive.
Until that becomes possible, India’s heatwave economy will continue to distribute its costs unequally, placing the heaviest burden on those with the least power to escape it.

Beyond the heatwave: Preparing for a hotter future
From green infrastructure and planning to the visitor experience and collaboration, the final part of the series looks at what a hotter future means for how horticulture operates, and why the sector is as essential to adaptation as it is exposed to the risk.
The question now is not how horticulture gets through the next heatwave, but whether it can build heat resilience into the way it operates, invests, designs and delivers landscapes.
But horticulture cannot do this alone. Heat is a challenge that reaches well beyond the sector, and preparing for it needs clear policy and leadership from government. That is currently missing: the National Heat Risk Commission’s report, A Heat Circuit Breaker for the UK, finds heat risk well documented but poorly governed, with no equivalent of the strategy, institutions and clear responsibilities that exist for flooding.
Following on from the first four parts of The Dirt’s five-part series, which examined the commercial cost of the summer’s heat and drought, the toll on staff, the impact on plants and the pressure on water, this final part looks ahead. Businesses adapted quickly, from working hours and watering to production and what they sell, but the summer also exposed structural weaknesses, from water security and infrastructure to the establishment and aftercare of plants. This article asks how horticulture can turn those challenges into opportunities, and what it will take to prepare the sector for a hotter future.
Resilience as an asset
The summer has brought a sharper focus on what climate resilience means for businesses operating in a hotter, more volatile climate. For many, that means practical changes to buildings, water management, irrigation, working practices and investment decisions.
David Denny, Director of Research & Knowledge Transfer at the Horticultural Trades Association (HTA), argues that the meaning of resilience itself is changing. “Traditionally resilience meant recovering after a difficult season, but now, with our changing climate it increasingly means designing businesses that can continue operating through sustained extremes.” A climate-resilient sector, he says, uses water as efficiently as possible, captures and stores rainfall, grows a broader range of climate-tolerant plants for warmer, wetter winters as well as hot, dry summers, protects staff and customers during extreme heat, and has the infrastructure to withstand both drought and flooding.
The same shift is under way in the markets horticulture serves. The property sector, closely tied to horticulture, is beginning to treat heat resilience as an asset-management issue. In a July 2026 article, Savills highlighted the importance of natural shading, green roofs, reflective materials, improved insulation and passive ventilation in reducing overheating, alongside cooling where necessary. It argued that adaptation should be considered across the property lifecycle, from design and construction through to operation and retrofit.
Savills’ August Market in Minutes: UK Commercial research went further, noting that the summer’s heatwaves had increased investor attention to climate resilience, while higher operating costs and weaknesses in older buildings were strengthening the preference for high-quality, climate-resilient assets. The research suggests that climate resilience is moving beyond an ESG consideration towards a core investment and occupational requirement. That matters for horticulture. If climate resilience increasingly affects the operating costs, attractiveness and long-term value of buildings and places, investment in the landscapes around them becomes part of that equation. The opportunity is to show that planting and green infrastructure are not simply environmental additions, but assets that help places function better in a hotter climate.
Norham Gardens, St Edmund Hall’s new development in Oxford, shows what building in resilience from the outset can look like. The Passivhaus buildings need no mechanical cooling. Mature trees have been kept, drought-tolerant planting placed in the most exposed spots, and swales, green roofs and a rainwater-fed pond manage water on site. Plants were established at a younger size so they can root more deeply and cope better with climate pressures. The scheme more than doubled student capacity while delivering an 88% biodiversity net gain, evidence that density and landscape need not compete.
Economics can work against that ambition. House price growth has slowed for four consecutive months, according to the Office for National Statistics, with prices falling in London and the South East as rising mortgage costs bite. As margins shrink, developers delay or shelve schemes, and the landscapers, designers and suppliers who would deliver more resilient landscapes lose work. Investment in resilience is hardest to justify just when the market is under pressure.
Even so, the case for green infrastructure is getting stronger. The HTA’s new Value of Green Spaces report highlights the role of trees and green infrastructure in helping towns and cities adapt to rising temperatures. The industry that grows, designs, plants and maintains those landscapes is therefore part of the infrastructure needed to prepare the wider built environment for a hotter future.
Trees provide cooling as well as shade, with the HTA report highlighting research showing that one large, sun-exposed tree can provide a cooling effect equivalent to around 10 air-conditioning units. Unlike portable cooling equipment, however, trees and green infrastructure need to be planned, planted and established well before the heat arrives.
That gives horticulture a dual role, and one few other sectors share. Like any business, it must adapt its own operations, as Denny describes. But its products are themselves part of the solution: the trees, plants and landscapes that cool towns, manage water and make places more resilient. Horticulture feels the effects of extreme heat as directly as any industry, yet it is also one of the few that can help everyone else adapt to it.
That role starts on its own doorstep. Garden centres, parks, gardens and other public-facing landscapes can showcase the practical value of shade, resilient planting, water management and green infrastructure, while nurseries, growers, landscapers and designers provide the plants, expertise and services needed to deliver them.
There is already evidence that this can have a practical benefit for horticultural businesses themselves. As explained earlier in this series, Stephanie Dunn, Managing Director of Frank P Matthews, told The Dirt that footfall at the nursery’s Tree Shop was not affected by the heatwave. The combination of trees, greenery and shade created a more comfortable environment for visitors, illustrating how the landscape around a business can itself form part of its resilience.
The opportunity often starts in the car park. Admittedly, how often do you arrive at a garden centre to find a large car park with almost no tree cover, and a surface that is already radiating heat before you have even walked into the centre? For an industry that sells trees and plants, there is a clear opportunity to demonstrate their value not only through what is sold, but through how its own sites are designed and managed.
Emma Howard Boyd, Chair of the National Heat Risk Commission, argues that green infrastructure should be considered part of this wider response. “Green infrastructure is another important example because it can provide benefits beyond a single site,” she says. “The horticultural industry can be part of the solution by providing more and healthier green spaces that have wider co-benefits beyond production.” Green infrastructure, she adds, can also be thought of as a measure that protects production itself from heat.
She adds that adaptation does not necessarily require major capital investment. Changes to work organisation, the use of shade and vegetation, better monitoring and incorporating heat resilience into normal investment decisions can all form part of the response.
Adapting the visitor experience
The impact of extreme heat extends beyond retail and production to gardens and attractions that rely on visitors. For these businesses, resilience is not only about maintaining the landscape or keeping people comfortable. It also means understanding how weather changes visitor behaviour and adapting the offer accordingly.
At the Eden Project in Cornwall, chief executive Andy Jasper says prolonged periods of good weather can make the beach a significant competitor, particularly for families. Eden responded deliberately, increasing its national profile and strengthening its summer programming as it approached its 25th anniversary.
“We wanted to increase our visibility, but also remind people what is unique about us and Cornwall and to give them compelling reasons to visit,” says Jasper.
That meant putting horticulture back at the heart of Eden’s story and taking it to new audiences, with its Bring Me Sunshine garden at RHS Chelsea, while drawing visitors to Cornwall with the Eden Sessions summer concerts and a programme for families. “We were very conscious that we needed to give people a really strong reason to choose Eden,” says Jasper. “That influenced both our programming and how we communicated it.”
The strategy appears to have paid off, with Eden recording one of its strongest summers in years despite the hot weather. For Jasper, this flexibility is becoming a fundamental part of managing botanic gardens and horticultural attractions in a changing climate.
“Climate resilience isn’t only about how we manage plants, landscapes, water or extreme weather. It is also about understanding how a changing climate changes visitor behaviour.”
Much of that behaviour is decided before visitors leave home, and the forecast can matter as much as the weather itself. Earlier this year, Chester Zoo coordinated a call from attractions including the Eden Project, RHS gardens and Blenheim Palace for the Met Office to review how forecasts are displayed on popular apps, warning that a single raincloud icon can suggest a washout even when much of the day is expected to be dry. Tourism consultancy Navigate, which works with more than 50 UK attractions, found that visits drop by an average of around 30% when an unfavourable weather icon appears. With around 70% of people checking the forecast before leaving home, how heat warnings are communicated may matter just as much as summers grow hotter.
For smaller gardens, adapting starts with reading visitor patterns. At Stockton Bury Gardens in Herefordshire, curator Tamsin Westhorpe has seen a clear shift. “There is definitely a trend of people visiting earlier in the day for more of a brunch,” she says. In response, the garden moved its café hours this year from 11am-4.30pm to 10.30am-4pm, and because all its food is made on site, it can switch its offer to suit the weather, an option not every garden has.
The season is shifting too. September was much busier this year, with many visitors saying August had simply been too hot, and Westhorpe expects it to become a much busier month, especially for workshops. She would also like garden clubs to consider group visits earlier in the year: “April is such a beautiful month but not historically popular with groups.”
She shares the concern about weather apps. “If people see rain they don’t come, for example when this might mean just a drop for half an hour in the day,” she says, encouraging visitors to look beyond the headline icon and dig deeper into the Met Office app, which she believes would help venues survive. Visitors can play their part as well: “We don’t see enough hats so we have started to sell them!”
The National Garden Scheme (NGS) is already seeing the change. This summer, some owners stayed open to offer shade while others considered cancelling in extreme heat, and some gardens have since moved their 2027 openings from the traditional afternoon slot to the morning. The NGS also planned to consult garden owners at the end of the season on how openings might need to evolve.
The experience of Eden points to a wider shift: resilience may increasingly depend on the ability to respond to weather in real time, from changing opening hours and programming to reconsidering where and when visitors spend time. As Jasper puts it, gardens also have a role in helping people understand what is changing and “inspire them with what they can actually do in their own gardens, communities and places”.
Garden retail: designing for the heat
Garden centres may sell far more than plants today, but plants and trees are still what customers most identify them with, and a key reason many visit. The demand is there: HTA figures show sales of hardy plants, shrubs and trees rose 20% in September once conditions eased, and Frank P Matthews saw demand for trees pick up strongly. Footfall at the company’s own Tree Shop also held up during the heatwave. A hotter climate is a reason to build on that identity, not move away from it.
Hospitality, though, is where much of the margin is, and adapting increasingly means rethinking it. Cafés and restaurants have become a central reason to visit, often delivering a higher gross margin than traditional garden retail, but they are also among the parts of the business most exposed to extreme heat.
That is already shaping investment. Yorkshire Garden Centres is considering air conditioning across its restaurants, while at Squire’s Garden Centres, Retail Buying Director Ricky Bowness says the air-conditioned parts of the business were “understandably popular” this summer. But cooling adds energy costs, so the challenge is to balance comfort, investment and running costs.
There is also an opportunity in how those spaces are designed. Speaking at the Garden Centre Association’s annual conference in January, Mary Portas OBE argued that garden centres are becoming one of the most relevant retail formats of the moment. In a world of global uncertainty, digital saturation and polarised discourse, she noted, people are gravitating towards the local, and towards places that feel grounded and human. Garden centres, she said, are “rooted in nature, wellbeing, patience, and growth, they encourage participation, not passive consumption”. They invite dwell time and conversation, and, in her words, “value-led retail creates resilience”. What she called soulful retail needs imagination and ambition to deliver.
A hotter climate gives that idea a practical edge. Horticulture’s own strengths, its trees, plants and shade, are exactly what can make a garden centre that grounded, human place on a hot day: somewhere to find a cool moment in the sun. And with a single large tree able to provide cooling equivalent to around 10 air-conditioning units, according to research cited in the HTA’s Value of Green Spaces report, planting should be at the heart of how garden centres plan for the heat, not an afterthought to air conditioning.
Some garden centres already lead the way. For others, it could mean tree-planted car parks, shaded terraces, tree-lined seating and planted courtyards around cafés and restaurants: spaces that cool visitors, showcase the plants on sale and turn the centre itself into a demonstration of what resilient planting can do. It would extend a role Denny says garden retailers have increasingly taken on over 2026: that of trusted advisor, guiding customers towards plants that can cope with drought and other climate extremes.
The importance of the wider supply chain
Preparing for heat also means looking beyond the nursery gate. A business can protect its own staff, stock and water supplies and still be exposed through its suppliers, its transport routes and its energy costs.
Extreme heat has already shown how far those risks can travel. Low water levels on major European rivers, including the Rhine and Danube, have reduced the loads barges can carry and pushed some freight onto road and rail, with knock-on effects for the movement of plants, growing media, containers and machinery. High river temperatures have also led to restrictions on nuclear output in France, where river water is used for cooling, a reminder that heat can disrupt energy supply as well as drive up demand.
The businesses best placed to cope are likely to be those that anticipate these risks rather than react to them: knowing which suppliers, routes and inputs are most exposed, where stock or alternatives could be secured early, and how disruption elsewhere would feed through to costs and delivery. It is the wider business system Howard Boyd urges businesses to consider, from suppliers and transport to stock and product quality.
Heat is of course not the only pressure on those supply chains. Since March, the conflict in the Middle East has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, pushing up energy, fuel, fertiliser and freight costs across horticulture. British Berry Growers reported fertiliser and crop protection costs up 30–40% and packaging up 10-25% since 1 March, while the NFU has warned of sharp rises in electricity costs for horticultural businesses. The two risks compound one another: the cost of cooling, irrigation and storage rises just as the weather makes them more necessary.
The businesses best placed to cope are likely to be those that anticipate these risks rather than react to them: knowing which suppliers, routes and inputs are most exposed, where stock or alternatives could be secured early, and how disruption elsewhere would feed through to costs and delivery. It is the wider business system Howard Boyd urges businesses to consider, from suppliers and transport to stock and product quality.
The supply chain also matters at the point where plants move from growers to gardens, landscapes and public spaces. Richard McKenna, Managing Director of Provender Nurseries, says the industry needs to recognise that responsibility for successful planting does not end when a plant leaves the nursery.
For McKenna, the answer is collaboration. Too often, he says, individual businesses are left to confront the same problems in isolation. He wants the industry to work together, and for that effort to reach beyond nurseries to the professional bodies representing landscapers, designers and landscape architects: the British Association of Landscape Industries (BALI), the Association of Professional Landscapers (APL) and the Landscape Institute (LI).
“We all grow plants, all differently, in different locations, with different customers. But fundamentally we’re all growers,” he says. “We want the best plants, with no disease or pests. We want to do it right and responsibly. Collaboratively, we are stronger.
Landscape architects and garden designers in particular need to be involved, he says, because it is the client who ends up paying for plants that either fail or flourish. Maintenance and proper irrigation should be built into schemes at the design stage, so that success is measured by whether plants thrive, not simply by whether they are planted.
Nurseries, he says, are good at watering and keeping plants alive. The risk comes after delivery. “We’ve had plants leave the nursery and be dead within three days, and it’s blamed on us for supplying poor-quality plants. In 30 or 35 degrees of heat, the care and maintenance after the plants leave our nursery isn’t something we’re responsible for. There are many parts of the puzzle that need joining up, not just the nursery.”
Tree planting and establishment
As public funding for tree planting grows, the industry has a chance to shape how success is measured. Stephanie Dunn has questioned whether tree-planting grants place sufficient emphasis on what happens after planting, arguing that funding too often focuses on the number of trees planted rather than how many survive and thrive.
McKenna shares that concern. The government’s new £53 million Community Trees Fund, announced on 30 September as part of a £79 million nature recovery package, will support the planting of up to 500,000 trees in England between April 2027 and March 2030. For McKenna, the real measure is how many are still alive a year later. “They’re chasing the numbers,” he says. If most of the trees planted are dead within a year, he asks, “what’s the point?”
For McKenna, it comes down to attitude. “If somebody spent £100,000 on a beautiful car, they’d change the oil and the tyres. They’d look after it. It’s about our attitude to things other people use, like parks.”
The HTA has made the same point. Welcoming the fund, Jennifer Pheasey, Director of Policy and Public Affairs at the HTA, said the trees must be climate-resilient and, “most critically, cared for”, and Denny has long argued that tree-planting initiatives must fund establishment and watering, particularly in urban areas. With the fund’s criteria still to be published, the sector has a window to press for aftercare to be built in from the start. The cost of getting it wrong is already known. During the 2022 drought and heatwave, more than 60% of newly planted trees were severely affected at the worst-hit sites, according to Forest Research.
For a sector increasingly asked to deliver green infrastructure, that is also an opportunity. Establishment, watering and long-term aftercare are services horticulture is well placed to provide, and many of the tools are products the industry already sells, from tree-watering bags and soil moisture sensors to drip irrigation and plants chosen for the site. Making the most of that means the industry communicating its value more loudly to clients, councils and funders, and being integral to planting projects from the outset rather than brought in at the end simply to supply plants. Planting in autumn rather than late spring would give trees a better start. Tying funding to how many trees survive, rather than how many are planted, would mean aftercare is budgeted and paid for from the start, rather than being the first thing cut. The expertise needed already exists across the sector, among growers and nurseries, arborists and tree officers, landscape architects, designers and landscapers, head gardeners, foresters and researchers, and in botanic gardens and arboretums, built up through long-term trials, living collections and the lessons of this summer.
The UK imported 85.5 million trees and shrubs worth £229 million in 2025, according to Defra figures reported by The Dirt. That is down by a third since 2023, but the average imported plant is now larger, pointing to a gap in domestic production of mature trees. The Strong Roots partnership of the Woodland Trust, the HTA, the National Trust and the RHS is calling on government to assess how many imported trees could be grown in Britain and to plan for more domestic production, so that nurseries have the confidence to invest, recruit skilled staff and reduce the pest and disease risks that come with imports.
Delivering that will mean working with government rather than waiting for it. The Community Trees Fund’s criteria are still to be set, the revised National Planning Policy Framework already asks developments to plan for tree planting and green infrastructure over their lifetime, and the National Heat Risk Commission is building its recommendations on evidence from organisations across the UK. Through trade bodies such as the HTA, the APL, BALI and the Landscape Institute, the industry can bring survival data and practical experience to the table.
Designing for climate change
Climate adaptation will increasingly shape what gets built. The revised National Planning Policy Framework, published in September, requires development plans to take account of extreme weather and long-term climate trends, from overheating, wildfire and drought to flood risk, water supply, biodiversity and landscapes. Proposals must consider climate impacts over a scheme’s lifetime, including surface water, overheating, green infrastructure and tree planting. For the landscape industry, that is a significant opportunity: it moves resilience upstream, into how places are planned and designed, and creates demand for the expertise to deliver it.
Howard Boyd wants the principle to go further. Writing for the UK Green Building Council (UKGBC), she says: “Every major public investment should be assessed against the climate conditions it will face over its lifetime, and that principle should apply equally to every major building investment and retrofit decision, public and private, and it should be embedded across government, from Treasury spending decisions to planning and infrastructure policy. That means writing resilience requirements into planning policy and building standards with the same seriousness currently given to carbon, rather than treating adaptation as a follow up conversation once mitigation targets are settled.” She also hopes heat resilience will become part of the Government’s ten-year plan for growth.
The challenge now is turning policy into practice. Liz Nicholson, Managing Director of Nicholsons, has discussed the framework widely, including at a recent workshop on the Oxford–Cambridge growth corridor. “I would not say the changes are in people’s consciousness yet in conversations I have had so far,” she says. Clients and developers rarely use the language of climate resilience unless they are councils or planners, and even those who want to act lack the tools: “Many developers do have their own standards but they have no way of measuring them and there is no standardisation of the standards!”
Tools are emerging to close that gap. Nicholsons’ elemental tool assesses the environmental and social impacts of landscape projects, from materials, soils and embodied carbon to biodiversity, water and social factors, across design, construction and aftercare. That lifecycle view will matter more as conditions change. How a landscape performs in the decades ahead depends on how soil is handled, materials are sourced, construction is carried out and the site is maintained, and clients will need to weigh the costs of maintenance, replacement and adaptation against the value of landscapes that keep performing.
For Nicholson, the purpose of design itself has to change. “Surely the days are gone where designers design for the aesthetic as a dominant narrative. Every design needs to deliver multiple ecosystem benefits.” But the industry cannot do it alone, and government is the missing partner. “We need regulation. We need planners to be asking for carbon reports on all development,” she says. She describes the designer as “the conductor of the orchestra”, though skills range from self-taught garden designers to landscape architects working on the urban realm, and sees an opportunity to fund the Landscape Institute and the Society of Garden & Landscape Designers (SGLD) to train them in sustainable design.
The question now is whether climate resilience can become a measurable part of how developments are designed, assessed and managed over their lifetime. If it does, horticulture will be central to delivering it.
The Royal Parks’ new Horticulture Vision offers a glimpse of that future at scale. Covering 2026-31 and around 5,000 acres across London’s eight historic parks, it focuses on diversifying planting, improving soil health and managing water more resiliently, with trials of drought-tolerant roses in Hyde Park, more exotic planting in Kensington Gardens and an agave trial with the RHS, all balanced against the parks’ historic character and the expectations of millions of visitors. A real showcase for horticulture, as alongside its focus on resilience, soil and water, the Vision is ambitious in its planting, proof that adapting to a hotter climate can be as inspiring as it is practical.
For Dr Linda Yueh CBE, Chair of The Royal Parks, the plan is also about who gets to see it. “Planting of this ambition is usually found behind a ticket barrier or a long journey out of London. Here it will be on their doorstep, free for everyone, Londoners and visitors alike.”
McKenna, who attended the launch in St James’s Park, believes the wider industry can learn from it. “Tens of millions of people go through the parks all the time, and they’re adapting to the future. I think we need to take a leaf out of the Royal Parks’ book. They’re being brave, bold and futuristic, really going for it. Maybe public spaces will show us what needs to be done.”
Changing gardens, changing expectations
How gardens are managed is changing too. At the National Trust, Sheila Das, Head of Gardens and Parks, has developed what she calls “Slow Gardening”, an approach built on observing, responding and working with nature rather than imposing fixed planting schemes or chasing instant visual impact. “Slow Gardening is about working with nature, not against it,” she says. “It’s ecological by design, combining sustainability, heritage, beauty, and visitor experience.” It does not mean abandoning historic planting, but questioning practices that may no longer be viable and making what she calls “conscious compromise” where necessary.
The approach is already reshaping Trust gardens. At Nymans, struggling rose beds have given way to a meadow mix that flourished without watering, feeding or heavy intervention. Cliveden is using no-dig systems to protect soil and save water, Sheffield Park and Garden is trialling drought-tolerant planting, and elsewhere vulnerable species and high-input bedding are making way for hardier alternatives and longer-lasting perennials. With more than 200 gardens and parks, each with its own history and conditions, the Trust can test what works where and give garden teams the confidence to decide locally, building a body of evidence the wider industry can learn from.
Changing planting also means bringing the public along, and Das wants visitors to see gardens develop rather than only the finished result. “Slow Gardening encourages everyone to engage with the process, not just the finished picture,” she says. “By showing visitors our process, including small wins along the way, we inspire practices that extend into private gardens, collectively creating wildlife corridors across the UK.”
The idea is spreading well beyond the Trust. The new Queen Elizabeth II Garden in Regent’s Park, created by The Royal Parks with landscape architects HTA Design and opened in April, deliberately resists the idea of an instant landscape. Designed as a climate-resilient slow garden, it will establish and mature over time, with naturalistic planting by Dr Noel Kingsbury, swales to manage rainwater, a tank storing run-off beneath a former water tower, crushed concrete reused as a growing medium and a projected 184% biodiversity net gain.
In Eastbourne, the change was to the planting palette itself, from traditional to more resilient. Its move from Victorian carpet bedding to drought-tolerant seafront planting initially met opposition. But after a year in which the new scheme thrived through hot, dry conditions, almost 70% of the 16,014 people who responded to an independent consultation preferred it. They did not want less ambition: design, planting and maintenance featured in 77.5% of written responses, colour, structure and visual impact still mattered, and sustainability, climate and water were mentioned in 40%. People will accept a significant change in planting style, provided it still delivers the qualities they value.
Others are adapting tradition rather than replacing it. Waddesdon Manor in Buckinghamshire intends intends to keep its High Victorian bedding displays, integral to the character of the house and gardens Baron Ferdinand de Rothschild created in the 19th century, despite losing some plants early this summer, says Suzie Hanson, Garden Manager at Eythrope and Waddesdon, and plans to make them sustainable with drip irrigation in the Parterre and Aviary.
Whether they reshape their planting or adapt tradition, these gardens share a conviction: horticultural quality and environmental responsibility are not a trade-off. By rethinking established practice, testing alternatives and letting visitors see change happen, they are showing what gardens in a hotter climate can be, and inspiring the millions who visit them to take those ideas home. It is horticulture’s dual role in action: adapting itself, and showing everyone else how.
Adaptation cannot happen in isolation
No business can adapt alone, but resilience need not wait for government either. The HTA has consistently argued that businesses cannot carry the full cost of adapting to a changing climate, and that investment in infrastructure and policy support will be needed alongside their own action. Meanwhile, some are already finding ways to work together on shared risks.
In the River Lark catchment in eastern England, growers and other agricultural businesses have explored sharing water during drought. Research involving the Lark Abstractors Group and Cranfield University modelled how sharing could reduce irrigation deficits and make better use of unused licensed capacity, with support from the River Lark Catchment Partnership, the NFU and the Environment Agency. It offers a model others could follow, with public and industry bodies helping to overcome technical and regulatory barriers.
The same thinking applies to the opposite extreme. At FarmED, a 107-acre demonstration farm in the Cotswolds, director Ian Wilkinson has restored the natural course of water across the land, building a series of small ponds, connecting channels and attenuation bunds that slow run-off after heavy rain and release it gradually, alongside a shallow scrape that holds floodwater and helps it soak into the subsoil (Land App, 2024). The village below the farm flooded in 2008. On its own, Wilkinson says, one farm’s work will make little difference, but “joined up across the valley on multiple farms… it just might”.
Working through a farm cluster also opens up funding from environmental land management schemes and private sources such as water companies and Biodiversity Net Gain. Larger growers could apply the same principle: holding water on the land when rain is heavy means less runs off, less soil is lost and more soaks into the ground, helping with both extremes rather than one.
Howard Boyd points to a further example of collective action in Accra, Ghana, where the Heat Awareness and Market Shade Infrastructure Initiative is developing shared, shaded and solar-powered market infrastructure to protect people working in extreme heat, alongside water, rest areas and space for storing and cooling produce. For horticulture, the more useful question is not simply who should pay for adaptation, but what businesses can achieve together by pooling resources and expertise, and where public or industry support could make those solutions viable.
Water, planning and investment
Water will remain one of the biggest tests of resilience. As the previous article in this series showed, 88% of businesses surveyed by the HTA said restrictions on mains or abstracted water would seriously harm or threaten their survival, yet investment in storage is held back by capital, land, planning and abstraction rules. Even Provender Nurseries, which has invested around £250,000 in water capture and storage, relied heavily on mains water this summer.
The task ahead is not only to secure water for horticulture but to manage it better across the wider landscape, capturing the intense rainfall that can overwhelm drainage only weeks before dry spells bring restrictions.
Building heat into business planning
Howard Boyd’s advice is not to wait for the National Heat Risk Commission’s recommendations. As the second article in this series set out, she suggests starting with practical steps, from a clear procedure for very hot days to reviewing working hours and knowing how heat warnings will trigger action, and looking at the whole business system rather than staff alone. Her wider point is to start with what businesses can control, identify where they need help, and build heat into normal business planning rather than treating it as an emergency.
Not all of it is about physical investment. Provender Nurseries has worked with the HTA and water companies to improve how water restrictions are communicated to customers, alongside its own investment in water infrastructure. Communication, coordination and shared information will matter as much as reservoirs and irrigation.
As the Commission puts it: “Heat is not just an environmental issue. It is a health issue, an economic issue and a security issue, and it belongs on every company’s risk register.”
The principle of assessing investment against the conditions it will face over its lifetime applies as much in the commercial world as in public policy. Every investment, retrofit, expansion, merger or acquisition should be tested for heat and drought risk. For horticulture, that could mean asking whether a new site has secure access to water, whether an abstraction licence will transfer with an acquisition and meet the business’s needs, whether a new glasshouse or restaurant can be kept at safe working temperatures, and whether stock and staff can be protected through repeated heatwaves.
Preparing for repeated extremes
Summer 2026 will not be the last of its kind. Some businesses kept trading and producing; others faced higher costs, lost sales, water restrictions and changing customer behaviour. All now face decisions about a climate that is becoming hotter, drier and less predictable.
“A flood has a perimeter. A storm has a track. Heat has neither. It is an invisible transfer of energy that moves through bodies, buildings, materials and networks all at once, and it does so silently,” writes the National Heat Risk Commission in its report. Yet unlike flooding, heat still has no framework setting out responsibilities, funding and coordination.
The 2022 heatwave was a warning. 2026 has shown what happens when extreme heat combines with drought, water restrictions, pressure on infrastructure and disrupted production. The Commission’s call for evidence, which closes on 30 October, will help shape its recommendations. For Howard Boyd, success would mean the UK is better prepared before the next major period of extreme heat, “with heat resilience built into decisions about infrastructure, investment, planning, buildings, public services and business operations”.
This series has attempted to show where the pressure falls: on sales and margins, on staff, on plants and production, and on water. It has also shown a sector already adapting, investing in water, changing how it works, rethinking planting and establishment, reshaping the visitor experience and finding ways to work together. The task now is to turn those individual responses into a shared, systematic approach to resilience.
“One of the clearest lessons from 2026 is that environmental horticulture is both vulnerable to climate change and essential to adapting to it,” says Denny. “The businesses growing trees and plants today are also helping create cooler towns and cities, greener homes, healthier communities and landscapes that are better able to cope with future extremes. Supporting the resilience of horticultural businesses is therefore an investment in the UK’s wider climate resilience.”
Horticulture is not just a sector exposed to climate risk. It grows, designs, plants and maintains the trees, landscapes and green spaces that will help towns and cities cope with a hotter future. That is its opportunity, but it will not be realised by businesses working alone. We need more collaboration across the supply chain, a stronger voice in planning and policy, investment in water and green infrastructure, and funding that values establishment and long-term care as much as planting.
What next?
The National Heat Risk Commission will publish its report, setting out practical pathways towards a heat-resilient UK, in summer 2027. Future phases of its work will include hearing directly from individuals, and the Commission’s website carries updates on how to get involved.
Closer to home, several developments in the coming months will matter to horticulture, from the funding criteria for Defra’s Community Trees Fund and the Health and Safety Executive’s review of workplace temperature rules to the Environment Agency’s drought outlook through to spring 2027.
In October, the HTA joined the Government’s Flood and Drought Resilience Taskforce, chaired by Emma Hardy MP, Minister for Water and Flooding, with Chief Executive Fran Barnes representing the sector. The HTA is using the role to press for a year-round approach to water resilience, a UK water resilience strategy and more accessible grants for the small and medium-sized businesses that make up more than 90% of the industry. It is a step in the right direction, giving horticulture a voice where water policy is being shaped.
In the meantime, the experience of this summer is too valuable to lose. Every landscape became a test plot this summer, and sharing what was learned across the industry, and building it into business planning, is one of the most powerful tools horticulture has as it adapts to a changing climate.
For growers and nurseries, that means recording how species and varieties performed across different soils and sites, building the kind of long-term evidence that Nick Dunn VMH, co-owner and former Managing Director of Frank P Matthews, says should guide changes to the range: “a sensible move through long-term experimentation”, rather than wholesale change in response to a single season. The knowledge of gardeners and head gardeners, working with plants every day, is invaluable. Horticultural work can be isolating, but it need not be. When it permits, attending conferences, seminars and masterclasses and sharing what they have seen is one of the best ways to pass that knowledge on. There is nothing quite like the energy of a room full of gardeners, as the Head Gardeners’ Conference at The Newt in Somerset and this year’s Hortistry masterclasses have shown.
Or, as McKenna so rightly put it: “We all grow plants, all differently, in different locations, with different customers. But fundamentally we’re all growers… Collaboratively, we are stronger.”
This series set out to capture an honest picture of where horticulture stands after summer 2026, in the industry’s own words and figures. That picture is only useful if it is shared. If you have found it valuable, please pass it on to colleagues, clients and anyone with a stake in horticulture’s future. And share your views with us: how this summer affected your business, what you are doing to prepare, and what you think needs to change.
The heat has passed for now. The decisions it demands have not.
From lost sales and delayed projects to rising costs and changing customer behaviour, the summer of 2026 has exposed the commercial consequences of extreme heat and drought for horticulture.

12:01
Image used for representational purpose only. Image Credit: ANI
Delhi recorded its wettest October day in four years on October 30, Friday, and also its highest monthly rainfall since 2022 .
The change in weather qualified the air to 'satisfactory' levels after the capital received 61.4 mm of rainfall in the last 24 hours.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) warned of additional thunderstorms with rains, issuing a 'red' alert across parts of the city like southeast Delhi, east Delhi, Shahdara, central Delhi, northeast Delhi, south Delhi, New Delhi, southwest Delhi, west Delhi, northwest Delhi and north Delhi.
On October 9, 2022, Delhi had recorded 74 mm of rainfall. That year, the city had recorded 128 mm of rainfall during the entire month.
The minimum temperature at Safdarjung, Delhi's base weather station, settled at 17.2 degrees Celsius, 1.1 degrees above normal, according to the weather body. The maximum temperature is expected to settle around 27 degrees Celsius.
Air quality deprecation due to pollution was brought under control due to rainfall with Delhi's Air Quality Index (AQI) standing at 90 at 9.30 am, placing it in the 'satisfactory' category, according to the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB).
Under the CPCB's AQI scale, readings between zero and 50 are classified as 'good', 51 and 100 as 'satisfactory', 101 and 200 as 'moderate', 201 and 300 as 'poor', 301 and 400 as 'very poor', and 401 and 500 as 'severe'.

Orange alert for rain and storms in 12 districts today:Cyclone Arnab drops temperatures by up to 5°C across 20 districts; Fatehpur records 10.5°C
Rajasthan witnessed heavy rain and a sudden drop in temperatures of up to 5 degrees Celsius on Thursday under the impact of Cyclone Arnab, bringing a spell of cold weather to several districts. The Meteorological Department has issued an orange alert for 12 districts, including Jaipur and Alwar, and a yellow alert for 16 districts for Friday.
Jaipur, Alwar and Karauli received light to moderate rain accompanied by strong winds, while gusty winds brought a chill to the Bharatpur, Jaipur, Ajmer and Kota divisions. Fatehpur recorded the lowest minimum temperature at 10.5 degrees Celsius.
During the past 24 hours, dense clouds covered Karauli, Bharatpur, Dholpur, Alwar, Dausa, Sawai Madhopur, Jaipur, Bhilwara, Ajmer, Nagaur, Tonk and several other districts, where light to moderate rain was recorded.
Maximum temperature in Barmer was 35.8 degrees Celsius
Due to the change in weather, the maximum temperature remained below 30 degrees Celsius in most parts of the state on Thursday, except in the western districts. Barmer recorded the highest daytime temperature at 35.8 degrees Celsius.
Jaisalmer recorded 34.2 degrees, Jodhpur 34.3 degrees, Jalore 33.7 degrees, Pali 33 degrees, Churu and Sri Ganganagar 32.7 degrees, Phalodi 32.6 degrees, Dungarpur 31.6 degrees, Bikaner 31.4 degrees and Chittorgarh 31.2 degrees Celsius.
Daytime temperature remained below 30 degrees Celsius in 10 cities
Clouds covered the sky throughout Thursday in Rajasthan, preventing sunshine. As a result, the maximum temperature remained below 30 degrees Celsius in 10 cities, including Karauli, Dausa, Sirohi, Jhunjhunu, Ajmer, Bhilwara, Tonk and Alwar. Consequently, these cities experienced a slight chill even during the daytime on Thursday.
Weather conditions in major districts of Rajasthan
Jaipur: Light clouds covered the Pink City throughout Thursday. Light drizzle occurred at several places in the afternoon, followed by heavy rain in the evening. Light to moderate rain was recorded at several locations across the city, including Tonk Road, Gopalpura, Malviya Nagar, Jagatpura, Ajmeri Gate and the Collectorate.
The rain and cold winds brought a sudden chill, leaving people shivering. The city's maximum temperature dropped by 4 degrees to 27.4 degrees Celsius on Thursday. The Meteorological Department has issued an orange alert for Jaipur for Friday, forecasting cloudy skies and light to moderate rain.
Heavy rain lashed several areas of Jaipur on Thursday evening.
Alwar: Intermittent drizzle continued in the city from Thursday morning. The rain brought a chill to the weather and provided relief from the heat. The maximum temperature in the city remained around 27 degrees Celsius. Cloudy skies and rainfall made the weather feel colder. According to the Meteorological Department, rain is also likely on Friday.
Light drizzle was reported in several parts of Alwar.
Udaipur: Clouds covered the city from Thursday morning, although the sun appeared intermittently for brief periods. The drop in temperature brought a slight chill to the weather. The daytime temperature was recorded at 30 degrees Celsius.
Udaipur remained cloudy throughout the day on Thursday.
Kota: The Meteorological Department had issued a rain alert for two days. Clouds covered the sky over the city on Thursday morning, although no rain was recorded. Sunshine prevailed in the afternoon. The city's maximum temperature was 30.9 degrees Celsius, while the minimum temperature was 21.6 degrees Celsius. The Meteorological Department has also issued a rain alert for Friday.
Kota remained cloudy throughout the day.
Jodhpur: Fluctuations in the weather continued in the city. The Meteorological Department had forecast rain for Thursday, but no rainfall occurred. The maximum temperature was recorded at 34.2 degrees Celsius, which was 0.4 degrees below normal. The minimum temperature was 20.4 degrees Celsius, which was 3 degrees above normal. The Meteorological Department has issued a yellow alert for rain on Friday.
Jodhpur remained cloudy throughout the day on Thursday.
Ajmer: Clouds covered the sky from Thursday morning. Cold winds kept the weather cool, while limited sunshine throughout the day provided relief from the heat. The city recorded a maximum temperature of 29.1 degrees Celsius and a minimum temperature of 18 degrees Celsius on Thursday.
Cool winds brought a noticeable chill to Ajmer.
Sikar: The impact of Cyclone Arnab was felt throughout Thursday. Clouds remained over Sikar all day, resulting in a drop in the maximum temperature. The Fatehpur weather station in Sikar recorded a maximum temperature of 30.5 degrees Celsius and a minimum temperature of 10.5 degrees Celsius. A yellow alert for rain has been issued for Sikar district for the next two days. Temperatures are likely to fall further in Sikar over the next 48 hours.
Cloudy skies prevailed in Sikar.
